document_title: EtherCAT — The Ethernet Fieldbus — EtherCAT Technology Group Brochure
version: ETG Brochure — Introduction to EtherCAT and the EtherCAT Technology Group
manufacturer: EtherCAT Technology Group (ETG) — Beckhoff Automation (originator). EtherCAT was introduced by Beckhoff in 2003 and is administered by the ETG, the world's largest fieldbus organization.

abstract: EtherCAT (Ethernet for Control Automation Technology) is a high-performance, low-cost, deterministic Industrial Ethernet fieldbus standardized as IEC 61158 Type 12, IEC 61784, ISO 15745-4 and SEMI E54.20. A single EtherCAT MainDevice (Master) drives a daisy-chained or branched network of up to 65,535 SubDevices (Slaves) over standard 100BASE-TX / 100BASE-FX cabling (EtherCAT G extends to 1 Gb/s; EtherCAT P combines 24 V power + data on one cable). The defining characteristic is on-the-fly processing — each EtherCAT Slave Controller (ESC) reads its input data and writes its output data into the Ethernet frame while the frame is still passing through the device's interface logic, at the wire speed of 100 Mb/s or 1 Gb/s. A single 1486-byte Ethernet frame can carry process data for thousands of devices, achieving cycle times below 100 µs and synchronization jitter below 100 ns via the Distributed Clocks (DC) sub-protocol. EtherCAT carries its datagrams as the payload of an Ethernet frame with EtherType 0x88A4, or alternatively encapsulated inside a UDP/IP packet on port 0x88A4 for non-EtherCAT path segments. Each EtherCAT datagram has a 10-byte header (Cmd + Idx + Address + Length + IRQ) and selects one of 13 addressing commands: NOP, APRD/APWR/APRW (Auto-Increment Physical), FPRD/FPWR/FPRW (Fixed Physical), BRD/BWR/BRW (Broadcast), LRD/LWR/LRW (Logical), ARMW (Auto-Increment Read Multiple Write), FRMW (Fixed Read Multiple Write).
external_pins: MII / RMII / RGMII to two integrated Ethernet PHYs per ESC (Port 0 = upstream toward MainDevice; Port 1/2/3 = downstream toward next SubDevice; redundant return on Port 0 for line/ring topology). Standard Fast Ethernet 100BASE-TX over Cat 5 with 8P8C / RJ-45 connectors, or 100BASE-FX over multimode fiber for long-distance segments.

PDI (Process Data Interface) on the application side of the ESC: choose one of (a) 8/16-bit asynchronous µC parallel bus, (b) 8/16-bit synchronous µC parallel bus, (c) SPI slave, (d) Digital I/O (up to 32-bit) with optional WD-strobe, (e) On-chip CPU bus (for ASIC integration). Includes IRQ output, INT/ECAT_DONE, and SYNC0/SYNC1 DC interrupt outputs.

EEPROM Interface (SII): 2-wire I²C-compatible (SCL, SDA) to an external 1-Kbit to 4-Mbit serial EEPROM holding the ESI (EtherCAT Slave Information) descriptor: Vendor ID, Product Code, Revision, Configured Station Alias, default SM/FMMU configuration, mailbox protocol bitmask.
RUN / ERR / LINK / ACT LED outputs per IEC 61784-2 (RUN = ESM state, ERR = AL error, LINK = PHY link, ACT = Rx/Tx activity).

EtherCAT P (single-cable variant): SE_VCC + SP_VCC dual 24 V US/UP power rails superimposed on the 100BASE-TX data pairs through ETG-defined coupling magnetics; 3 A per rail; one M8 4-pin connector replaces the conventional 4-conductor power + 4-conductor data setup.
package: EtherCAT Slave Controllers are typically delivered as ASIC (e.g. Beckhoff ET1100 in QFN56 / BGA128, ET1200 in QFN48, ET1815/ET1816 BGA), FPGA IP cores (Intel, Xilinx, Altera, Lattice), or integrated into automation SoCs (TI Sitara, Renesas RZ/N, Infineon XMC4800, Microchip LAN9252, etc.). MainDevice implementations run on standard PCs / industrial PCs / embedded controllers with any standard Ethernet MAC + PHY (no special hardware required).
supported_topologies: Mixed combinations of all the above

modes_of_operation.name: Cyclic process-data exchange (Op state)
modes_of_operation.description: MainDevice cyclically circulates one or more frames carrying LRD/LWR/LRW datagrams that touch the entire process-image of all SubDevices; cycle times typically 1 ms down to <100 µs.

modes_of_operation.name: Mailbox communication (acyclic)
modes_of_operation.description: MainDevice/SubDevice exchange variable-length messages through mailbox SyncManager channels (SM0 = MBox-Out, SM1 = MBox-In) carrying CoE / SoE / EoE / FoE / AoE protocols.

modes_of_operation.name: Distributed Clocks synchronization
modes_of_operation.description: ARMW datagram propagates the reference clock (ESC of first DC-capable SubDevice) to all DC-capable SubDevices; offset + drift compensation yields <100 ns jitter across the whole network.

modes_of_operation.name: Cable Redundancy (Ring + dual NIC)
modes_of_operation.description: MainDevice with two Ethernet ports drives the network as a ring; on cable break the segment auto-divides into two healthy line segments, no SubDevice loss.

modes_of_operation.name: Hot Connect / Hot Swap
modes_of_operation.description: Defined groups of SubDevices may be added or removed from the network during operation without disturbing the cyclic exchange of the remaining SubDevices.

key_features: On-the-fly frame processing: every ESC reads its inputs and writes its outputs into the Ethernet frame as it passes through the device's MAC, with only ~1 µs of forwarding delay per node. This is the foundational principle that lets one frame service thousands of nodes in one wire trip.
Up to 65,535 SubDevices per network (16-bit Configured Station Address space); 4 GB total Logical Address space (32-bit) shared by all SubDevices via FMMU mapping.

Performance: 1000 distributed digital I/O processed in 30 µs; 100 axes with 8 bytes each in 100 µs; bandwidth utilization typically >90 % on the wire vs. <5 % for switched standard Ethernet at the same rate.

Distributed Clocks (DC): nanosecond-class synchronization across the whole network; SYNC0 / SYNC1 output pulses per SubDevice are aligned to a common System Time; jitter <100 ns measured between SubDevices several hops apart.
Flexible topology: line, tree, star, ring, drop line, and mixtures — all on standard 100BASE-TX Ethernet physics, up to 100 m between nodes, 100 km+ with fiber.

Single Ethernet frame can carry the process data of an entire network: header (14 B) + EtherCAT header (2 B) + N × Datagram (10 B header + 1..1486 B data + 2 B WKC) + FCS (4 B), with a maximum useful payload of ~1486 B per frame.

10 addressing modes via Cmd field: NOP (0x00), APRD (0x01), APWR (0x02), APRW (0x03), FPRD (0x04), FPWR (0x05), FPRW (0x06), BRD (0x07), BWR (0x08), BRW (0x09), LRD (0x0A), LWR (0x0B), LRW (0x0C), ARMW (0x0D), FRMW (0x0E).

Working Counter (WKC): each datagram has a 16-bit WKC field that every addressed SubDevice increments by a deterministic amount (+1 on successful read, +2 on successful write, +3 on successful read-write). MainDevice compares the returned WKC against an expected value to confirm that every commanded SubDevice executed.

EtherCAT State Machine (ESM): six states — Init → PreOp → SafeOp → Op (+ optional Boot for firmware download). Application Layer Control (AL Control 0x0120) requests; AL Status (0x0130) confirms; AL Status Code (0x0134) reports.

FMMU (Fieldbus Memory Management Units): up to 8 per SubDevice; each maps a region of the network-wide Logical Address space (32-bit) onto a region of the local 64-KByte ESC memory at bit granularity. This is what makes LRD/LWR datagrams work efficiently — many SubDevices contribute to one logical-addressed datagram.

SyncManager (SM): up to 8 channels per SubDevice; each is configured as either a mailbox channel (handshake mode, atomic write-then-read) or a process data buffer (1-buffer / 2-buffer / 3-buffer mode with overrun protection).

Application protocols on mailbox: CoE (CANopen over EtherCAT — re-uses the entire CiA 301/4xx CANopen object dictionary and PDO/SDO model), SoE (Servo Drive Profile / IEC 61800-7), EoE (Ethernet tunneled over EtherCAT for legacy IP traffic to SubDevices), FoE (Firmware-Over-EtherCAT for SubDevice flash update), AoE (ADS routed messaging).

Safety over EtherCAT (FSoE — IEC 61784-3-12): an additional safety frame layered on the mailbox transport for SIL 3 / Cat 4 / PL e applications; black-channel principle means the underlying EtherCAT network is not safety-rated, only the FSoE end-points.
EtherCAT G (gigabit) and EtherCAT P (power + data on a single cable) are upward-compatible extensions of the base spec, sharing the same protocol layers above the PHY.

MainDevice independent diagnostic interface: a dedicated read-only command set (FPRD on selected ESC registers) lets any external diagnostic tool walk the network and read CRC counters, link state, port counters, ESM state of every SubDevice without disturbing the cyclic exchange.
transaction_summary: EtherCAT communication consists of (a) cyclic process-data exchange in state Op, driven by LRD/LWR/LRW datagrams targeting the network-wide Logical Address space, and (b) acyclic mailbox communication in states PreOp/SafeOp/Op driven by FPRD/FPWR targeting fixed SubDevice mailbox SyncManager regions. Each Ethernet frame may contain one or more EtherCAT datagrams chained back-to-back (the Next bit in the datagram header indicates 'another datagram follows'). The MainDevice originates every frame; SubDevices only insert/extract data on the fly and forward; the last SubDevice loops the frame back through Port 0 toward the MainDevice, which then verifies the Working Counter of every datagram.
data_model_summary: Each SubDevice exposes a 64-KByte local ESC memory containing: (1) hardwired ESC control/status registers at 0x000-0x0FFF, (2) DPRAM for process data + mailbox at 0x1000-0xFFFF. The MainDevice configures: SM0/SM1 = mailbox (typical 128-256 B in/out), SM2/SM3 = process data (Outputs to SubDevice, Inputs from SubDevice), FMMU0..FMMU2 = logical→physical mapping. The application above the mailbox exposes a CoE Object Dictionary (CANopen-style: Index 0x0000-0xFFFF × Subindex 0x00-0xFF) reachable via SDO over CoE.
overview: EtherCAT extends the Ethernet standard so that a single Ethernet frame can be used as a periodically circulated 'process data train' that visits every SubDevice on the network. The frames are forwarded through each SubDevice's two-port ESC at full 100 Mb/s wire speed; while passing through, the ESC's hardware-implemented FMMU + SyncManager + DPRAM logic reads the bits addressed to this SubDevice (for output process data) and writes the bits the SubDevice has produced (for input process data) directly into the frame. The on-the-fly mechanism removes both the per-node store-and-forward latency of switched Ethernet (typically 5-20 µs per hop) and the per-frame framing overhead of one-frame-per-device protocols, yielding a usable bandwidth efficiency that approaches the theoretical limit of the wire. The MainDevice runs on any standard Ethernet NIC; no special hardware is required on the controller side. The SubDevice side is a dedicated ESC ASIC or FPGA IP (Beckhoff ET1100/ET1200/ET1815, Microchip LAN9252, Intel/Xilinx/Lattice EtherCAT IP cores, Renesas RZ/N, TI Sitara ICSS_EMAC, etc.). The 13-command addressing scheme (Cmd 0x00-0x0E) covers Auto-Increment (used during start-up when stations are unaddressed), Fixed Physical (post-addressing), Broadcast (status queries to all devices), Logical (process-data via FMMU), and the two Read-Multiple-Write variants used for Distributed Clock propagation.
block_diagram_components: MainDevice software stack (configuration tool + cyclic engine + diagnostic interface) running on a standard PC / embedded controller; uses any standard Ethernet NIC.
Standard Ethernet PHY + MAC (no EtherCAT-specific silicon on the MainDevice side).
EtherCAT cable (Cat 5 or better, up to 100 m between nodes, 100 km+ with fiber).

EtherCAT Slave Controller (ESC) ASIC or FPGA, with 2-4 integrated 10/100 Ethernet ports, FMMU array (typically 8), SyncManager array (typically 8), Distributed Clock unit, EEPROM interface, PDI to local µC.
Per-SubDevice local microcontroller running the application firmware and the slave stack (ESM handler, mailbox protocol handlers — CoE/SoE/EoE/FoE/AoE — and the application object dictionary).
External SII EEPROM (1 Kbit to 4 Mbit) holding the ESI descriptor.
Optional Safety SubDevice running an FSoE stack on top of the standard SubDevice stack.
Optional EtherCAT P coupling magnetics for single-cable power+data installations.
use_cases: Industrial machine control (CNC, robotics, packaging, semiconductor wafer handling, printing)
Multi-axis motion control (servo drive networks, EtherCAT CoE DS402-style drive profile)
High-density distributed I/O (digital + analog + temperature + pressure across hundreds of nodes)
Measurement systems (oscilloscope-style data acquisition with nanosecond-aligned distributed sampling)
Functional-safety I/O networks (FSoE, SIL 3 / Cat 4 / PL e)
Test and measurement (semiconductor ATE, end-of-line test cells)
Automotive test rigs and HiL (hardware-in-the-loop) simulators
Wind / hydro / process automation (oil & gas, water treatment, mining)
EtherCAT Automation Protocol (EAP) — plant-floor MainDevice-to-MainDevice communication across machine cells
process_technology: Implementation-defined: ESC ASICs are typically 90 / 65 / 55 / 40 nm CMOS. FPGA IP cores target any modern fabric (28/20/16 nm). Brochure-level spec does not pin process technology.

revision_history.description: Public introduction of EtherCAT by Beckhoff Automation.
ETG founded to promote and standardize EtherCAT as an open technology.
EtherCAT becomes an international IEC standard (IEC 61158 Type 12 + IEC 61784 CPF 12).
ETG releases EtherCAT P spec — 24 V US + 24 V UP power superimposed on the data pairs.
1 Gb/s and 10 Gb/s variants announced, preserving the same protocol above the PHY.
Updated marketing + technical overview brochure presenting EtherCAT and the ETG.

topology_summary: Daisy-chain (line) is the dominant topology; the MainDevice's frame enters Port 0 of the first SubDevice, passes through every ESC on the way out via Port 1 (and is forwarded internally on the wire), reaches the last SubDevice, and is automatically looped back upstream through the unused ports of every intervening SubDevice (because each ESC closes the loop on any port that has no active link partner). The result is one logical bus that traverses every device twice (once going out, once coming back) on the same cable. Tree / star variants are formed by SubDevices that integrate 3 or 4 ports rather than 2. Ring topology (used for cable redundancy) uses two MainDevice NICs and closes the cable loop. Up to 65,535 SubDevices per logical bus; the only practical limit is the per-cycle frame size + cable propagation delay.
package_summary: EtherCAT is a wire-level + frame-level + register-level specification. Connector / cabling mechanicals follow IEEE 802.3 100BASE-TX (Cat 5 / 5e UTP, 8P8C / RJ-45, or M8 / M12 / M23 industrial connectors) or 100BASE-FX (SC / LC / MTRJ fiber). EtherCAT P adds ETG-specified coupling magnetics and an M8 4-pin connector that combines 100BASE-TX data plus US + UP 24 V rails.
